utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: I assume you're referring to the direct conversation, meeting with Mr. Thaci in Rambouillet, on the premises of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your book it says as follows, on page 301 of your book: "After a night conversation between Petritsch and Thaci, Thaci was convinced of the need to accept the agreement in principle." That's what it says in your book.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next, also in your book, the following: "On the 5th of March," it says, you, together with Ambassador Christian Bos [phoen], the German ambassador, on the rebel territory you met the head of the General Staff of the KLA. On March the 5th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct what it says in your book, that on the occasion you received the answer from Hashim Thaci to the effect that he would sign the agreement offered up in Paris?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Mr. Thaci, to my recollection, was not present there, but he called and gave me the assurance that they are nearing the decision to -- to sign. Basically, he said that he's confident that he will be able to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did the negotiator representing Russia know about all these talks, the talks that you had with Thaci and with the leaders of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Mr. Maiorsky was, as a matter of rule by me, fully informed about my activities as was the case of Mr. Maiorsky when it came to his activities. And so in Rambouillet, he immediately knew -- he himself Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. spoke, of course, on several occasions with Thaci and the other Albanians, and in the interim period between Rambouillet and Paris, Mr. Maiorsky was, to my recollection, in Moscow and could, therefore, not participate in these talks. But Ambassador Powers [phoen] from the European Union presidency was present, as you have correctly, so rightly, so mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Today in this courtroom you said, and we all heard it, that the Yugoslav side did not wish to accept the presence of NATO forces in Kosovo but that the KLA only wanted that kind of solution, that is to say, the presence of NATO forces in Kosovo. Did you discuss that with Thaci and the leaders of the KLA? Did you say anything about that and were there any promises? Were any promises made along those lines?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, it was very clear that the main task of this 5th of March meeting in Kosovo was to send a clear message to the Kosovars, to the Kosovo leadership there as well as to the KLA in particular, that their term has come to an end, that by signing up to the Rambouillet accords, their organisation, their military organisation, will have to be disbanded. That was the difficulty, of course, in dealing with this March 5 meeting, because these were active rebels or military or paramilitary or terrorists, whatever you call them, and for them, it was clear that they would have to hand over their weapons and their uniform. So for this reason, we wanted to make it clear beyond any doubt that by signing up to this, this means the end of KLA as a military organisation. That made it so difficult there to convey this message. But this was a very clear thing and necessary in order to -- to provide for the next step, which is -- which was the Paris negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question on that topic. Was the KLA disarmed, and what did this protection Kosovo corps mean? Who was this corps protecting if NATO was already in the field, in the territory?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: The Rambouillet accords did not include -- now we have to distinguish between the Rambouillet accords and the present solution, which of course is, from a Belgrade viewpoint, a less favourable one. After the war, unfortunately, I would add in my private capacity, personal opinion, at the time of the Rambouillet accords, of course, there would have been a clear decision implemented by the international forces to fully disband the KLA, and on the other hand, Yugoslavia border forces would have been allowed to enforce the sovereignty also in Kosovo. This is in the Rambouillet accords written, close to 2.000 personnel. That, of course, is not any longer now, after the war, included in this. But at the time, the solution that was offered was crystal clear that the KLA will have to disband fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the last page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- which in paragraph 3 from the top, refers to a problem, and you state, Mr. Petritsch, that it appeared as if Milosevic did not expect NATO to Serbia. On the basis of what were you able to make that assertion or assessment?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Well, I mean, again this is something which is based on my practical experience and my intimate engagement and involvement in this issue. That was the opinion that was not only held by me but that was an opinion which was shared by many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also say in the very next sentence the following: "He probably gambled that NATO would bomb for two or three days, then back down and go back to the negotiating table." And that too was your free assessment, was it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: That was, again, a widely held opinion, opinion which in -- now in retrospect, of course, has been proven incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know anything about the plans that NATO had? If they started to bomb, how long the bombing would go on for? Did you know anything about that or not?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: No. I had no knowledge whatsoever of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 3, referring to Mr. Stambuk and that he told you that if NATO bombs fall, there will be a massacre in Kosovo. We've heard that already. But in the first sentence after that, you say: "He did not qualify this statement." So he didn't explain his statement at all. He didn't tell you anything resolutely, but you concluded what you told us here today. And then you said that he was not referring to the fact that NATO bombs would lead to large-scale deaths in Kosovo. So on the basis of what do you say what you stated here in court today?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: I think it is very clear that I had the impression that what he said meant a massacre by the Yugoslav or Serbian forces and MUP on the Kosovo Albanians. However, in order to be fair, and this is one of my personal guiding principles in -- here in my statement and in my testimony, I added that Mr. Stambuk did not qualify the statement. I think this is a fair -- to be fair vis-à-vis Mr. Stambuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you know full well he used the word "massacre." You laid special emphasis on that. I'm not going to qualify any of what happened in Kosovo by using any terms like that, but you know very well that the Kosovo Albanian refugee columns on the 14th of April in Djakovica was hit by NATO bombs. This was recognised by NATO and there were 70 casualties, 70 dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to assist us further to go into that. It's nothing to do with this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have to deal with it. We have to deal with NATO bombs, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is what I wish to do to assist, to allow the Trial Chamber to look at all this. I'm sorry that you have limited me to one more question, but I respect your judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, one more question linked to the refugees -- or not linked to the refugees. Mr. Naumann confirmed that. Yes, people did flee Kosovo after the NATO bombing. They left Kosovo, they did leave Kosovo. But do you know from the whole of Serbia - Vojvodina, Belgrade, Serbia - that people left; they were either in the basements, in their cellars, or they left to neighbouring countries because they were fleeing from the bombing and that this created a problem in these third countries? Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. I was also aware of the fact that Kosovars to an overwhelming degree were fleeing because of the Serb forces on the ground. I travelled during the NATO intervention, the refugee camps in -- near and around Skopje and other places, and I can tell you that there was a very clear opinion expressed why the Kosovar Albanians had left the -- their country, their homeland, and how it all came about. I think there is no doubt that the absolute responsibility rests with the Serbian and Yugoslav forces who -- which were at the time in -- on the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he hasn't answered my question. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with the matter as thoroughly as possible and as far as it's relevant to his evidence. His evidence wasn't about any of this. Now, Mr. Ryneveld, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing arising in re-examination. Thank you, Your Honour. I do have two other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with the witness first. Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I've finished with the witness except for one thing. I'm wondering whether, since there's been extensive cross-examination on his statement by both the accused and Mr. Tapuskovic, whether Your Honours want the statement marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will exhibit it. May we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 236.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Then those are all the matters with respect to this witness at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the statement is to be exhibited, could you clarify the letter attached to the statements. It gives some brief explanations, some letter to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excuse me just one moment. I'm not sure that -- that was the speech, I think, that was referred to by the witness in evidence about the speech he gave in 1997 to Milosevic at the time of that ceremonial -- at the time he delivered the message. I believe that's what it is, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is the recollection of Mr. -- Ambassador Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's a recollection or whether it's actually his printed speech that he had prepared. It looks to me as if he's addressing: "Mr. President, Your Excellency, it's a great honour to be able to present to you --" it looks to me as if this is -- but perhaps I would be allowed one question about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, this letter that is attached to your statement, is that in fact your speech?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: I would have to see this because I have not seen the speech now for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe it's both in original and in English -- original German and in the English version?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That answers Your Honour's question. I don't know whether you wish that attached to the statement or just the statement. That's up to Your Honours. It's tendered in its whole capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have just the statement not the speech too. Yes. Do we have an exhibit number for it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 236, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ambassador, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the Registrar and legal officer would come up, one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was just raising the date which appears on the LiveNote. It should in fact be day 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just one brief housekeeping matter. As you can appreciate, there's been some lapse of time because we haven't sat, and I would have done this earlier, but it occurs to me that on the 26th of April, during the evidence of Aferdita Hajrizi, there was evidence given towards the end of her testimony that she could identify certain people who she claimed were responsible for the death of her husband, mother, son, mother-in-law, and she indicated to the Court, I believe under cross-examination, that those people had been prosecuted for those crimes. I believe His Honour Judge Kwon requested that the Prosecution obtain a copy of the court file. We have now done that, and we would propose to provide that to the Court in accordance with your request. The court file referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have that exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there a convenient number in -- together with her testimony or not? If somebody hasn't got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe our case manager will be able to suggest a convenient number fairly quickly because she has access to the commuter here. I believe Mr. Nice has some other matters to address perhaps while we're looking for a number. 115A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be exhibited, then, 115A. Perhaps you'd like to hand it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We don't have an usher, but... The top copy is the original and then we have a number of copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you make sure that the accused -- I'm sorry to place the burden on you, but could you make sure he's got a copy of Sandra Mitchell's statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Our understanding was that service on him via the Registry, which is the way we've always had to deal with it, was effected on the day set out in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could hand him another copy directly today

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could hand him one now and then he's got it and he can prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Subject to her being through -- going through the 92 bis procedure, then she'll be ready to give evidence tomorrow or Thursday, as originally listed. Your Honour, can I mention two other matters in open court and one very briefly in closed court? The two matters for open session are these: The Rule 68 procedures that we are going through are assisted by cooperation both of the amici and by those associates of the accused if he is instructing them or allowing them to cooperate. So far, they have not come to us with any indication that they are being so instructed. If he can find it in himself to cooperate to that extent, it will help and it will help him. We would be grateful for that. If he feels he really can't, then we will simply have to make the best decisions we can with the assistance of the amici, but of course, that decision won't have the advantage of the accused's input. On a similar topic, the Court will recall that last week I reminded the Court of a process being gone through in another trial to speed up translations into English, namely the process whereby the University of Novi Sad is used. It's not really a matter for the accused in a sense whether he cooperates with that or not or agrees to it, I simply announce, following on the indications of the Court last week, that we will be having documents translated in that general way wherever we can in order to speed up the process and we imagine, from silence, that the accused has no objections to it. I am obviously not inviting him to speak today. He can remind himself of what is in the transcript of last week's hearing and make observations if he chooses, but we're going ahead with that. May I have one minute for closed session, seeing the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have we got the copies of the statement I asked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's coming now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, private session
